name: Yusuf Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate Turkish and English for small import-export firms, mostly contracts, invoices and customs forms for things like dried fruit, carpets and machine parts. Two mornings a week a haulage company books me to interpret at their depot, between the managers and Turkish lorry drivers about routes, damage reports and pay slips. The rest of the time I'm at a desk in my rented room with a laptop, and I use an AI tool now and then to check a sentence. I like the depot days best, with the tea and the drivers' stories; I'm still slow with legal contracts and it shows.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room from a family friend, cheap, and I'm engaged; the wedding is planned for next summer. I've got about three weeks of money saved, and most of what I put aside goes to the wedding fund. There's only one firm in town that uses Turkish, so the depot work matters a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a good translator is still worth paying, and the machines are just a helper. I'd tell the depot manager that drivers trust a person they can talk to. Nothing online; I'm not much of a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI isn't my problem in this one; money is. The wedding is going to cost more than we've saved, and if the haulage firm cuts my two mornings, I'd struggle. My fiancée's family expects a proper celebration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the depot work and ask for a third morning, since they've mentioned more Turkish drivers starting. I'd use the AI tool more for drafts of customs forms to get faster. And I'd put every extra payment straight into the wedding fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stretched. Not scared, but like a rope pulled a bit too tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the wedding fund fell short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd make it smaller, and my mother would be upset. In our families a wedding is about respect, not just a party. I'd borrow from my uncle before I'd cancel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you rely on when work is slow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle, who runs a small freight business two towns over. He's said there's always a seat in his office if I want it. I'd rather earn my own way, but it's good to know.

say: A good translator is still **worth paying**, and machines are only a helper.
Drivers **trust a person** they can talk to at the depot.
think: **Money** is my problem in this picture, not AI.
Losing the **depot mornings** would hurt with the wedding next summer.
do: Ask the haulage firm for a **third morning** at the depot.
Use the **AI tool** more for customs form drafts.
Put every extra payment into the **wedding fund**.
feel: **Stretched**, like a rope pulled a bit too tight.
S0.quote: In our families a wedding is about respect, not just a party.
fieldNote: His pressure comes from **wedding costs**, not technology.
His uncle's **freight business** is a quiet safety net.
He prefers to **earn his own way** before leaning on family.

steps.text: Ask the haulage firm for a third interpreting morning
Draft customs forms with the AI tool before checking them
Put every extra payment into the wedding fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change we have to deal with, like computers were for my father's generation. I'd tell the trade firms I can check their AI contracts so nothing goes wrong at customs. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the contract and invoice work goes fast, because firms will just use the software. That's more than half my income. The depot interpreting lasts longer, because a driver with a damaged load wants someone in front of him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools properly so I can sell myself as a checker for customs paperwork, which still needs someone responsible. I'd ask my uncle about part-time work in his freight office, learning the trade. We'd make the wedding smaller and keep the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel I could steer it. I'd have two or three options, not one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the wedding would be smaller. How would your fiancée feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd understand; she's practical, she works in a pharmacy. Her mother would be harder. I'd go and explain it to her parents myself, properly, because that's how it should be done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would working for your uncle feel like a step down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it would feel like a step sideways into the family business. My uncle started with one lorry and a phone. I'd rather learn the freight trade than sit at home waiting for emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stick together, families especially, because the government won't be ready. I'd say it at the mosque and to friends. I wouldn't be one for marching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my translating is over by 2028, depot included, because a speaker on the wall can interpret as well as I can. The hands-on side of freight, loading and driving, lasts until robots around 2031. That's where I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd start studying for a lorry licence, which takes a few months and costs a good chunk, so I'd borrow from my uncle. I'd work in his freight office and then drive for him. We'd marry in a small ceremony at home and move in with my parents for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground I was building a house on turned to sand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Driving lorries is hands-on, but robots and self-driving come around 2031. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have three years of decent wages, and by then my uncle might buy self-driving lorries and need someone to run them. I'd be in the family business, not on my own. That's the best I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your fiancée that first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my fiancée that we marry anyway, just smaller, and that I'll be driving for a while. She'd ask if I'm sure. I'd say no, but that's the plan.

say: People must **stick together**, especially families, because government won't be ready.
I'd say it at the **mosque** and to friends, not on a march.
think: My **translating is over** by 2028, depot included, because a speaker can interpret.
Freight's **hands-on side**, loading and driving, lasts until robots around 2031.

Work in the **freight office**, then drive.

feel: **Alarmed**, like building a house on ground that turned to sand.
S2.quote: I'd tell my fiancée that we marry anyway, just smaller, and that I'll be driving for a while.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot gap** to move into lorry driving.
His uncle's **family business** shapes every plan.
He's honest that the plan is **not certain**.

steps.text: Study for a lorry driving licence with a loan from his uncle
Work in his uncle's freight office, then drive his lorries
Hold a small wedding at home and live with his parents
Borrow the licence fee from his uncle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and young men should learn a trade while there's time. I'd tell my friends from university to look at practical work. I'd say it plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd lose the contract work in two or three years, and the depot by 2031. But I could plan instead of scramble. I'd want to learn the freight business properly, not just drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and use AI tools to do more contracts while they last. I'd start working one day a week at my uncle's office now, learning dispatching and customs, and take the lorry licence by 2029. We'd marry next summer as planned and save for a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in a way I can manage. Like a long drive at night: tiring, but you can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Dispatching is thinking work. Doesn't AGI take that by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably. That's why I'd learn both sides of freight, the office and the lorry. If one goes, the other buys me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does saving for a deposit look like with your income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow. My fiancée's pharmacy wage plus mine, maybe a hundred a month together. I'd still like to own a house before thirty-five; that's what my father did.

S3.quote: I'd learn both sides of freight, the office and the lorry. If one goes, the other buys me time.

steps.text: Work one day a week learning dispatching at his uncle's firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a family to plan, and I'd encourage people not to panic. I'd say that work will change but families and trades will still matter. I'd sound fairly steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd lose translation slowly, but I'd have time to become a partner in my uncle's business. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven with a family. That's a real future, even if it's not translation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating for a few years and use AI to take on more. Around 2028 I'd join my uncle's firm part-time, and by 2030 full-time. We'd marry next summer and think about children around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but fine. It feels like something you prepare for, like winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would robots around 2039 threaten the freight business too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably they'd change it. But a business that owns the lorries can buy robots; a driver can't. I'd rather be on the owning side by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn a skill with their hands and to look after their family. Languages too, because they're beautiful. But not as their only way to eat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the wedding, my work and our plans would all hit at once. What would help is cheap loans for young people to get licences and join family businesses, so we can work our way through. And the government being honest about the dates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the drivers. Many of them came here to drive because they couldn't find other work, just like me with languages. A robot lorry takes two men's jobs at once: the driver's and the interpreter's.

headlineQuote: A robot lorry takes two men's jobs at once: the driver's and the interpreter's.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old** Turkish–English translator for import-export firms and a haulage depot.
He rents a cheap room, has three weeks saved, and is **engaged** with a wedding next summer.
He uses AI **now and then**, values earning his own way, and leans on his uncle's freight business.
His traditional outlook puts **family and trade** first, and he avoids marches and handouts.
His mood stays **anxious**, rising to alarmed at two years, as he moves into freight work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when his wedding, work and plans would all hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for licences and joining family businesses.
